title: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
title_ar: الحكم في ظل عدم اليقين: الاستدلالات المختصرة والتحيزات
key_findings: Proposes three judgment heuristics (representativeness, availability, adjustment-and-anchoring) that are usually useful but produce systematic, predictable errors.
Representativeness explains neglect of prior probabilities (base rates), insensitivity to sample size, misconceptions of chance and illusory validity.
Availability explains frequency misjudgments driven by ease of recall, imaginability and illusory correlation.
Anchoring: estimates stay biased toward an initial value, even an arbitrary one, because adjustment is insufficient.
athar_applications: Canonical vocabulary for the bias library and debrief cards.
Anchoring and sample-size items are safe, robust targets for case mechanics; base-rate items need careful framing (see Koehler 1996, Gigerenzer & Hoffrage 1995).
limitations: Mostly word problems with student samples; ecological validity contested (Gigerenzer; Koehler).
Describes errors, not interventions; says little about how to train people out of them.
Later replication work supports anchoring strongly but not every effect associated with the program.

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
title_ar: التفكير السريع والبطيء
key_findings: Popular synthesis of the heuristics-and-biases program framed as two modes of thinking (fast/intuitive vs slow/deliberate).
Its Chapter 4 on social/behavioral priming relies on studies that later analyses judged weakly replicable (see ATH-SRC-0502, ATH-SRC-0503).
Core judgment findings (e.g., anchoring) have fared better in multi-lab replication than the priming chapter (see ATH-SRC-0504).
athar_applications: Useful as framing for designers, but never cite it alone for a claim; trace each claim to the primary study and its replication status.
System 1/System 2 is a teaching metaphor for debriefs, not a validated mechanism to assess.
limitations: Trade book, not peer-reviewed; mixes robust and non-replicated findings.
Author publicly conceded over-reliance on underpowered priming studies.
Dual-process framing itself is debated in the literature (not verified in this session in detail).

title: Reconstruction of a Train Wreck: How Priming Research Went off the Rails
key_findings: Analyzed 31 studies from 12 articles cited in Chapter 4 ('The Associative Machine') of Thinking, Fast and Slow; all reported significant results despite median observed power of about 57%.
Computed an R-Index of 14 and concluded the studies should not be treated as evidence for the claimed effects.
Kahneman replied in the comments, conceding: "I placed too much faith in underpowered studies."
athar_applications: Teaching case for ATHAR's own epistemic humility: even famous experts over-trust weak evidence.
Can inspire a meta-level case where the player audits a 'too-perfect' set of studies (all significant, small samples).
limitations: Blog post, not peer-reviewed; R-Index is a heuristic diagnostic, not proof of fabrication.
Applies to the priming chapter, not to the whole book.

title: Behavioral Priming: It's All in the Mind, but Whose Mind?
license: CC BY (Creative Commons Attribution License; version not confirmed on page)
key_findings: With automated infrared timing (N=120), the classic elderly-priming walking-speed effect did not appear.
In a second study (N=50, 10 experimenters), slower walking appeared only when experimenters expected it; manual stopwatch timing introduced expectancy-driven error.
Shows how an investigator's expectations can contaminate measurement, not just interpretation.
athar_applications: Model for an 'investigator-expectancy' case: a witness or timer whose measurement bends toward what they expect; the fix is blind or instrumented measurement.
Debrief link: confirmation bias acts on data collection as well as on reasoning.
limitations: Single replication pair; small Study 2 sample.
Addresses one priming paradigm, not all priming research.

title: Investigating variation in replicability: A "Many Labs" replication project
key_findings: 13 effects tested across 36 samples (N=6,344); 10 replicated consistently, 1 weakly, 2 failed (flag priming, currency priming).
All four anchoring items replicated in every sample with weighted d between about 1.17 and 2.42, larger than the original aggregate d=0.93.
Gain/loss framing replicated but smaller than original (d 0.60 vs 1.13); sunk cost (0.27) and retrospective gambler's fallacy (0.61) close to originals.
Lab vs online and US vs international setting did not substantially moderate effect sizes.
athar_applications: Anchoring, framing, sunk cost and gambler's fallacy are evidence-safe targets for ATHAR cases; social priming is not.
Supports teaching 'replication status' as part of each bias card.
limitations: Effects tested in short, decontextualized formats; large d values partly reflect the simplicity of the anchoring paradigm.
WEIRD-heavy samples; no Arab-region labs (gap for ATHAR).

title: A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect
key_findings: 23 labs, N=2,141, preregistered: ego-depletion effect d=0.04 with 95% CI including zero.
athar_applications: Do not design 'mental fatigue' mechanics or claims around ego depletion.
Illustrates the difference between popular psychology and replicated findings for the meta-science module.
limitations: Tests one sequential-task paradigm; debate continues about other paradigms.

title: How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: Frequency formats
title_ar: كيف نحسّن الاستدلال البايزي دون تعليم: صيغ التكرارات
key_findings: Across >2,800 solutions, Bayesian-consistent answers rose from about 16% with probability formats to about 46-50% with natural-frequency formats, without any instruction.
Argues the mind is adapted to frequencies acquired by sequential sampling; frequency formats reduce computation and make base rates implicit.
Relative frequencies (percentages) did not help; the benefit depends on natural sampling structure.
athar_applications: Present all probabilistic evidence in ATHAR (e.g., test reliability, base rates of suspects) as natural frequencies ('out of 1,000 people...') with icon arrays.
Base-rate cases should teach representation change, not formula memorization.
limitations: Even with frequencies, roughly half of participants still erred.
Debate with heuristics-and-biases authors over whether the effect reflects 'natural sampling' or simply clearer nested-set structure (not resolved in this session).

title: Meta-analysis of the effect of natural frequencies on Bayesian reasoning
key_findings: Synthesized 35 articles and 226 performance estimates over 20 years with a bivariate mixed-effects model; confirms a natural-frequency facilitation effect.
Short-menu (joint-event) formats and visual aids were among the strongest facilitators, in both probability and frequency formats.
Methodological choices (scoring criteria, incentives) and individual differences (numeracy, expertise) moderate performance.
athar_applications: Pair natural frequencies with a visual (icon array / tree) in every base-rate puzzle.
Score process (did the player build the reference class?) rather than only the final number.
limitations: Pooled effect numbers not extracted in this session (abstract elided); verify in full text before quoting magnitudes.
Tasks are mostly textbook Bayesian problems, not rich narrative evidence.

title: Teaching Bayesian reasoning in less than two hours
key_findings: A short computerized tutorial teaching people to re-represent problems as frequencies was compared with traditional Bayes-rule training across 2 studies.
Representation training produced a larger immediate learning effect and better temporal stability than rule training; transfer to new problems was comparable.
athar_applications: Strong evidence that a brief, interactive representation lesson (frequency trees) can be built into an early ATHAR case and re-probed weeks later.
Supports 'teach the representation, not the formula' design rule.
limitations: Lab tutorial with university students; retention intervals and effect sizes not extracted here.
Near-transfer (Bayesian textbook problems); far transfer to narrative evidence untested.

title: Heuristic Decision Making
key_findings: Defines heuristics as efficient processes that ignore part of the information; whether they perform well is an empirical question about the environment.
Reviews business, medical and legal evidence that simple heuristics can match or beat information-hungry models, especially when predictability is low and samples small.
athar_applications: Avoid teaching that intuition/heuristics are always 'bad'; debriefs should ask when a shortcut fits the environment.
Supports cases where a simple rule (e.g., checking one highly diagnostic cue) beats collecting every clue.
limitations: Ecological-rationality claims depend on environment structure; formal models are not easily taught to teens.
Ongoing debate with heuristics-and-biases school.

title: The base rate fallacy reconsidered: Descriptive, normative, and methodological challenges
key_findings: Argues the base-rate fallacy is overstated: people generally use base rates, to a degree that depends on task structure and representation.
Mechanically applying Bayes' theorem to label answers wrong is inappropriate when model assumptions (e.g., relevance of the base rate, the reference class) are unchecked.
athar_applications: Every ATHAR base-rate case must make the reference class explicit and defensible; otherwise the 'correct' answer is contestable and the case is unfair.
Debrief should discuss which base rate applies, not only the arithmetic.
limitations: Target article from 1996; later meta-analytic work (ATH-SRC-0507) refines the picture.
Commentaries (in BBS) not reviewed in this session.

title: Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises
title_ar: انحياز التأكيد: ظاهرة واسعة الانتشار بأقنعة متعددة
key_findings: Catalogs forms of confirmation bias: restricting attention to one hypothesis, pseudodiagnosticity (ignoring how likely the data are if the hypothesis is false), preferential treatment of supporting evidence, positive-case testing, overweighting confirming instances, expectation-driven perception, primacy and belief perseverance.
Notes that some 'biased' choices in the Wason selection task are partly legitimate tests, so not every pattern is pure failure to falsify.
Links the bias to real-world harms such as witch trials and persistent ineffective medical practices.
athar_applications: Each case should include at least one clue that is consistent with every suspect (non-diagnostic) to reveal pseudodiagnosticity.
Interface element: 'How likely is this clue if your suspect is innocent?' prompt.
limitations: Narrative review, not meta-analysis; umbrella term covers heterogeneous mechanisms.
Klayman & Ha (ATH-SRC-0512) show positive testing can be rational.

title: Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
key_findings: Many behaviors labeled confirmation bias are better described as a positive-test strategy: testing cases expected to have the property of interest.
The strategy is often a good heuristic under realistic conditions, but produces systematic errors in specific task structures; optimal strategy depends on the task.
athar_applications: Do not penalize players simply for testing their favored hypothesis; penalize failing to run a test that could falsify it when such a test is available and cheap.
Design cases where the rule/truth is broader than the obvious hypothesis (2-4-6 structure) so only negative tests reveal it.
limitations: Formal analysis with abstract tasks; mapping to narrative investigations requires design judgment.

title: The case for motivated reasoning
title_ar: الحجة لصالح الاستدلال المدفوع بالرغبة
key_findings: Accuracy goals increase effort and use of appropriate strategies and can reduce some biases (but not always).
Directional goals bias which memories, rules and beliefs are accessed and how evidence is evaluated, while people retain an illusion of objectivity.
Motivated reasoning is constrained: people need a justification that would persuade a dispassionate observer; when they cannot build one, they accept unwanted conclusions.
athar_applications: Build cases where the player has a stake (a likeable suspect, a friend NPC) to create directional goals ethically.
Require players to write the justification for their accusation; Kunda's 'plausible justification' constraint means explicit justification tasks can expose motivated reasoning.
limitations: Review of 1980s literature; mechanisms debated; accuracy incentives can sometimes worsen performance.

title: Myside Bias, Rational Thinking, and Intelligence
key_findings: Myside bias (evaluating evidence and testing hypotheses in ways favoring prior opinions) shows very little relationship with intelligence across many paradigms.
Avoiding myside bias is therefore a rational-thinking skill not captured by IQ tests.
athar_applications: High-ability players are not protected; myside challenges must appear at every difficulty tier.
Measure myside separately from puzzle-solving speed/accuracy.
limitations: Short review; magnitude of correlations varies by paradigm.

title: Rational thinking and cognitive sophistication: Development, cognitive abilities, and thinking dispositions
key_findings: Examined developmental trends on 5 rational-thinking tasks: denominator neglect, belief bias, base-rate sensitivity, resistance to framing, otherside thinking.
Performance related consistently to age, cognitive ability (intelligence, executive function) and thinking dispositions (actively open-minded thinking, superstitious thinking, need for cognition).
athar_applications: Evidence that these sub-skills are still developing in the ATHAR age range; difficulty should be age-banded.
Thinking dispositions (AOT) are measurable separately and can be tracked as outcomes.
limitations: Cross-sectional; Canadian school samples; not a training study.

title: Cognitive Reflection and Decision Making
title_ar: التأمل المعرفي واتخاذ القرار
key_findings: Introduces the 3-item Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT), measuring the tendency to override a compelling but wrong intuitive answer.
CRT scores predict time and risk preferences relevant to expected utility and prospect theory.
athar_applications: Design pattern: 'lure' items with a fast, wrong, attractive answer; but do not copy CRT items, which are now widely known.
CRT-style items are a weak outcome measure for ATHAR because of familiarity and numeracy confounds.
limitations: Only 3 items; widely circulated online so prior exposure inflates scores (exposure effect not verified in this session).
Correlates strongly with numeracy; construct debated.

title: Debiasing Decisions: Improved Decision Making With a Single Training Intervention
title_ar: تقليل التحيز في القرارات بتدخل تدريبي واحد
publisher: Policy Insights from the Behavioral and Brain Sciences 2(1), 129-140
key_findings: Two longitudinal experiments: a single session of a serious game or an instructional video reduced six biases (Exp 1: bias blind spot, confirmation bias, fundamental attribution error; Exp 2: anchoring, representativeness, social projection).
Games, which gave personalized feedback and practice, outperformed videos: bias reduction of at least about 32% immediately and about 24% at 2+ months (videos about 19% at both points).
Authors report effects generalized to untaught problem formats and contexts.
athar_applications: Strongest direct analogue for ATHAR: interactive play with explicit bias instruction + personalized feedback beats passive video.
Template: teach bias -> practice in context -> immediate feedback -> delayed re-test in a new format.
limitations: Funding commonly reported as a US government debiasing program (IARPA Sirius) - not verified in this session; adult samples; outcomes are bias measures similar in kind to training (near-to-medium transfer).
Sample sizes not extracted in this session.

title: Debiasing Training Improves Decision Making in the Field
title_ar: التدريب على تقليل التحيز يحسّن القرارات في الميدان
key_findings: N=290 graduate students; a one-shot debiasing game was received either before or after an unannounced business case modeled on the Challenger launch decision.
Trained participants were 29% less likely to choose the inferior, hypothesis-confirming solution.
Analysis of write-ups suggests the gain came from less confirmatory hypothesis testing; evidence of transfer to a different domain and format.
athar_applications: Most decision-relevant evidence that game-based debiasing can transfer to an unannounced, realistic case: ATHAR should test learning with unannounced cases in a different surface domain.
Use 'stealth' transfer probes rather than announced bias quizzes.
limitations: Assignment via natural schedule variance, not full randomization; one case; graduate business students.
Authors call it promising, not conclusive; no independent replication verified in this session.

title: Fake news game confers psychological resistance against online misinformation
key_findings: Bad News: players adopt a fake-news producer role and learn six manipulation techniques.
Self-selected sample of 14,266 pre-post pairs, no control group: reliability ratings of fake items dropped (average d about 0.52); real-item ratings barely changed.
Authors list limitations: no randomized control, unrepresentative sample, no retention test, no real-world behavior measure.
athar_applications: Perspective-taking mechanic (play the manipulator) is engaging and age-appropriate if fictionalized.
ATHAR should not repeat the design weaknesses: use controls, matched true/false items and discrimination metrics.
limitations: Weak design (pre-post, no control, self-selection); see ROC reanalysis ATH-SRC-0523.

title: Good News about Bad News: Gamified Inoculation Boosts Confidence and Cognitive Immunity Against Fake News
key_findings: 2x2 mixed design with gamified control, N=196, 18 fake headlines.
Bad News improved detection of manipulation techniques versus control and increased confidence, but only among participants who updated in the correct direction.
athar_applications: Track confidence alongside accuracy: calibrated confidence is a separate outcome.
limitations: Small sample; outcome mostly fake items, so discrimination vs general skepticism not separable (see ATH-SRC-0523).

title: Long-term effectiveness of inoculation against misinformation: Three longitudinal experiments
key_findings: Bad News vs Tetris control (N=170 in the reported experiment): fake news rated less reliable after inoculation.
With regular re-testing the effect remained stable for at least 3 months; without such re-testing it decayed and was no longer significant at 2 months.
Item memorization did not explain the effect (Exp 3).
athar_applications: Spaced re-encounters ('boosters') appear necessary for retention; ATHAR seasons should revisit each skill at increasing intervals.
Retention must be measured with delayed probes, not end-of-case scores.
limitations: Outcome is reliability ratings, subject to the response-bias critique (ATH-SRC-0523); small samples per experiment.

title: Psychological inoculation improves resilience against misinformation on social media
key_findings: Five short videos on manipulation techniques (emotional language, incoherence, false dichotomies, scapegoating, ad hominem).

Seven preregistered studies: six RCTs (N=6,464) and a YouTube field study (N=22,632); improved technique recognition, confidence, trustworthiness discernment and sharing decisions, across political spectrum.
athar_applications: Technique-level (not topic-level) teaching is the transferable unit: ATHAR should name manipulation techniques and re-present them in new topics.
Short (sub-2-minute) prebunk inserts can precede cases.
limitations: Outcomes measured shortly after exposure; real-world behavior largely proxied; co-author affiliations (possible industry partner) not verified - check funding/conflicts in full text.
AUDIT 2026-10-27: licence confirmed as CC BY 4.0 via Europe PMC (PMC9401631) and OpenAlex (gold OA); rights corrected from UNKNOWN (attribution required).

title: Gamified inoculation interventions do not improve discrimination between true and fake news: Reanalyzing existing research with receiver operating characteristic analysis
title_ar: تدخلات التحصين المُلعَّبة لا تحسّن التمييز بين الأخبار الصحيحة والزائفة
key_findings: Reanalyzed five Bad News / Go Viral! studies with ROC curves that separate discrimination from response bias.
With comparable true and fake items, the games did not improve discrimination; players became more conservative, rating everything as less reliable.
Argues earlier mean-rating comparisons overstated effectiveness and that interventions may be counterproductive if they breed blanket distrust.
athar_applications: ATHAR must score credibility judgments with signal-detection metrics (hits and false alarms on matched true/false evidence), never only 'rejected fake items'.
A player who distrusts everything has not learned evidence evaluation; cases need trustworthy evidence that must be accepted.
limitations: Reanalysis of existing datasets; inoculation authors have responded and debate continues (responses not verified in this session).
Does not test video-based prebunks in ATH-SRC-0522 to the same extent (not confirmed here).

title: Lateral Reading and the Nature of Expertise: Reading Less and Learning More When Evaluating Digital Information
title_ar: القراءة الجانبية وطبيعة الخبرة
publisher: Teachers College Record 121(11) (volume/issue as encoded in DOI)
key_findings: Think-aloud study of 45 experienced users: 10 PhD historians, 10 professional fact checkers, 25 Stanford undergraduates evaluating live websites.

Historians and students read vertically and trusted surface cues (logos, domain names); fact checkers left the site quickly to see what others said about it (lateral reading) and reached more warranted conclusions in a fraction of the time.
athar_applications: Evidence documents in ATHAR should have provenance that can only be checked 'off-page' (other in-world sources), rewarding lateral reading over close reading.
Expertise in a domain does not transfer automatically to source evaluation: teach the strategy explicitly.
limitations: Small expert-novice sample; descriptive, not an intervention; US web context.

title: Lateral reading on the open Internet: A district-wide field study in high school government classes
key_findings: District-wide matched-control field study: teachers given professional development delivered six 50-minute lateral-reading lessons in a mandated high-school government course; treatment students (n = 271) vs regular classrooms (n = 228).
Multilevel models showed treatment students grew significantly more in judging the credibility of digital content (ERIC abstract).
athar_applications: Evidence that lateral-reading instruction is feasible at school scale for teens; read full text for effect sizes before citing magnitudes.
limitations: Matched (not randomised) design; US urban district; effect sizes not extracted from the abstract.

title: Students' Civic Online Reasoning: A National Portrait
key_findings: 3,446 US high school students, six constructed-response tasks with live internet: performance poor on all.
96% never discovered a climate site's fossil-fuel ties; about two-thirds could not distinguish news from ads; over half took an anonymous video as strong evidence of voter fraud.
Students relied on surface cues (design, domain, About page, volume of information).
athar_applications: Baseline expectation: most teen players will start with surface-cue evaluation; early cases should target this explicitly.
Constructed-response tasks with live search are a model for ATHAR's in-world 'open search' assessment.
limitations: US sample; no Arabic-language equivalent found in this session (gap).

title: Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education
title_ar: إطار الثقافة المعلوماتية للتعليم العالي
authors: Association of College and Research Libraries (ACRL)
key_findings: Six frames: Authority Is Constructed and Contextual; Information Creation as a Process; Information Has Value; Research as Inquiry; Scholarship as Conversation; Searching as Strategic Exploration.
Revisions were approved by the ACRL Board on 2026-09-02 (check the revised text before final use).
athar_applications: 'Authority is constructed and contextual' maps to ATHAR's source-credibility mechanic (an expert witness is authoritative only within their domain).
NC license: may be cited and paraphrased, but its text cannot be embedded in the commercial product.
limitations: Conceptual framework for higher education, not an empirically validated intervention; criticized in library literature as hard to assess (not verified here).

title: When and where do we apply what we learn? A taxonomy for far transfer
title_ar: متى وأين نطبّق ما نتعلمه؟ تصنيف للنقل البعيد
key_findings: The far-transfer debate stalled because studies did not specify along which dimensions transfer was tested; proposes a 9-dimension framework (content and context dimensions).
A single 'far transfer effect size' oversimplifies; across about a century of research, transfer can be substantial under some conditions, but many conditions remain untested.
athar_applications: Each ATHAR transfer probe should be tagged on the taxonomy's dimensions (knowledge domain, physical/temporal/functional/social context, modality) so claims are precise ('transfers across topic but not across modality').
Use the taxonomy to plan a ladder of probes from near to far.
limitations: Conceptual framework; not itself evidence that transfer occurs.
Dimension names beyond 'content' and 'context' not re-verified in full text this session.

title: Teaching critical thinking for transfer across domains: Dispositions, skills, structure training, and metacognitive monitoring
title_ar: تعليم التفكير النقدي من أجل النقل عبر المجالات
key_findings: Four-part model for teaching CT for transfer: (1) dispositional preparation for effortful thinking, (2) explicit skills instruction, (3) training in the structural features of problems and arguments, (4) metacognitive monitoring.
Structure training is what lets learners recognize when a skill applies in a new context.
athar_applications: Every case debrief should name the abstract structure ('this was a base-rate problem disguised as a witness story') to support recognition in new surfaces.
Pair skills with disposition-building (curiosity, willingness to slow down).
limitations: Position paper; empirical support is drawn from other studies; Halpern also authors a commercial test (HCTA), a potential interest to note.

title: Instructional Interventions Affecting Critical Thinking Skills and Dispositions: A Stage 1 Meta-Analysis
key_findings: 117 studies, 20,698 participants, 161 effects; average effect size 0.341 with substantial heterogeneity.
Type of CT intervention and its pedagogical grounding explained about 32% of variance; research design explained little.
Concludes CT gains are unlikely through implicit expectation: CT objectives should be made explicit.
athar_applications: ATHAR must make reasoning objectives explicit (name the skill, show the principle) rather than hoping play alone teaches it.
Combine explicit principles with immersion in the case (the 'mixed' approach in Ennis' typology; to verify in full text).
limitations: Mixed study quality; many outcomes are general CT tests; age groups heterogeneous.

title: Strategies for Teaching Students to Think Critically: A Meta-Analysis
title_ar: استراتيجيات تعليم الطلاب التفكير النقدي: تحليل تجميعي
key_findings: 341 effect sizes from quasi- or true-experimental studies using standardized CT measures; weighted random-effects mean g = 0.30 with heterogeneity.
Both generic and content-specific CT instruction work across levels and disciplines.
Opportunities for dialogue, exposure to authentic or situated problems, and mentoring had positive effects.
athar_applications: Three evidence-backed levers for ATHAR: dialogue (structured argument with NPCs/peers), authentic problems (realistic cases), mentoring (guided feedback).
Expected effect sizes are modest (~0.3 SD): marketing claims must be calibrated accordingly.
limitations: Heterogeneous studies; standardized tests may not capture case-specific skill; few game-based studies.

title: Does College Teach Critical Thinking? A Meta-Analysis
key_findings: CT skills and dispositions improve substantially over a typical college experience.
Specific curriculum-wide efforts to improve CT do not necessarily produce incremental long-term gains beyond that.
athar_applications: Maturation and schooling raise CT anyway: ATHAR impact claims need comparison groups, not pre-post only.
limitations: College samples; magnitudes not extracted in this session.

title: Does Far Transfer Exist? Negative Evidence From Chess, Music, and Working Memory Training
title_ar: هل يوجد نقل بعيد؟ أدلة سلبية من الشطرنج والموسيقى وتدريب الذاكرة العاملة
key_findings: Three meta-analyses (chess, music, working-memory training): small-to-moderate effects that shrink as design quality improves (e.g., active control groups).
Authors extend doubts to spatial training, brain training and video games, concluding far transfer of general cognitive skills rarely occurs.
athar_applications: ATHAR must not claim that solving mysteries improves general intelligence, memory or school grades.
Target specific, teachable reasoning principles and measure transfer of those principles, with active-control comparisons.
limitations: Concerns general cognitive-ability transfer from domain practice, not explicit principle instruction (where Morewedge/Sellier and Sedlmeier show more transfer).

title: A Developmental Model of Critical Thinking
title_ar: نموذج نمائي للتفكير النقدي
key_findings: Argues CT programs ignore developmental research; frames CT as built on second-order cognition (meta-knowing).
Identifies three forms of meta-knowing: metacognitive, metastrategic, and epistemological.
athar_applications: Track epistemological understanding (is knowledge certain, opinion, or evaluated claims?) as a developmental outcome alongside skills.
Metastrategic prompts ('which strategy did you use and was it the best?') belong in every debrief.
limitations: Theoretical model; developmental levels are broad; Kuhn's later empirical argument-skill programs not verified in this session.

title: Cognitive and Interpersonal Features of Intellectual Humility
title_ar: الخصائص المعرفية والاجتماعية للتواضع الفكري
key_findings: Four studies with a new Intellectual Humility (IH) Scale: IH related to openness, curiosity, tolerance of ambiguity and low dogmatism.
High-IH participants judged attitude-changing politicians less as flip-floppers and were more attuned to the strength of persuasive arguments.
athar_applications: Sensitivity to argument strength is the behavioral marker of IH that ATHAR can observe in play (does the player's confidence track evidence quality?).
Reward 'changing your mind for good reasons' explicitly; avoid framing revisions as failure.
limitations: Self-report scale; correlational; US adult samples.

title: Predictors and consequences of intellectual humility
key_findings: Review synthesising definitions and measures of intellectual humility; identifies the common element as a meta-cognitive ability to recognise the limits of one's beliefs and knowledge.
Reviews influences on IH (e.g., relationship security, social coordination), its benefits and drawbacks for decisions, relationships, science and society, and early attempts to boost it.
athar_applications: Entry point for an expert review of whether IH can be trained and measured behaviorally.
limitations: Abstract read via PubMed (2026-10-27 gap-fill); review mostly of adult, Western samples.

title: Metacognition and cognitive monitoring: A new area of cognitive-developmental inquiry
title_ar: ما وراء المعرفة والمراقبة المعرفية
publisher: American Psychologist 34(10), starting p. 906 (volume/issue/start page from DOI; end page not verified)
key_findings: Foundational paper arguing young children know little about cognitive phenomena (metacognition) and do relatively little monitoring of their own memory and comprehension; proposes a model of the adult-like metacognitive knowledge and monitoring that development moves toward (ERIC abstract).
Commonly cited for the distinction between metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive experiences (standard use; distinction not visible in the short abstract).
athar_applications: Basis for confidence ratings and 'what don't I know yet?' prompts in cases.
limitations: Theoretical, 1979; only the short ERIC abstract read; knowledge/experience distinction still needs full-text check.

title: Teaching Critical Thinking: Some Lessons From Cognitive Science
title_ar: تعليم التفكير النقدي: دروس من العلوم المعرفية
key_findings: Six lessons: CT expertise is hard to acquire; practicing CT skills themselves builds them; transfer must be practiced; some theory helps; diagramming arguments (argument mapping) helps; students tend toward belief preservation.
athar_applications: Argument-map mechanic: the player's accusation is built as a visual tree of claims, evidence, objections and rebuttals.
Explicit transfer practice: the same structure re-appears in a different case surface.
limitations: Essay drawing on cognitive science; the author developed commercial argument-mapping software (Rationale), a potential interest; meta-analytic evidence for argument mapping not verified in this session.

title: Abduction (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
title_ar: الاستدلال الافتراضي (الموسوعة الفلسفية لجامعة ستانفورد)
publisher: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University)
key_findings: Modern 'abduction' usually means inference to the best explanation (IBE): ampliative and non-monotonic (new premises can defeat a conclusion).
Peirce's original abduction concerned generating hypotheses; the modern sense concerns justifying them.
Van Fraassen's 'bad lot' objection: the best available hypothesis may be the best of a bad lot; comparative versions of abduction survive it.
Explanation and Bayesian updating may be complementary: explanatory considerations can inform priors and likelihoods.
athar_applications: Two separate ATHAR sub-skills: hypothesis generation (Peircean) and hypothesis selection (IBE).
Every case should include a 'none of the above / not enough evidence' option to train the bad-lot check.
Non-monotonicity justifies late-revealed evidence that overturns an earlier good conclusion.
limitations: Philosophical reference; empirical psychology of abduction only briefly covered.

title: Inference to the Best Explanation
title_ar: الاستدلال إلى أفضل تفسير
key_findings: Argues we infer to the hypothesis that would best explain the evidence and that explanatory 'loveliness' can guide toward truth.
2nd edition adds a chapter on explanation and Bayesian reasoning and develops contrastive explanation ('why this rather than that?').
athar_applications: Contrastive questions ('why was the window broken from inside rather than outside?') are a strong case-prompt pattern.
Debrief can distinguish 'most explanatory' from 'most likely' and show when they diverge.
limitations: Philosophical argument; contested (see SEP critiques); not an empirical learning study.

title: Executive Functions
title_ar: الوظائف التنفيذية
key_findings: Three core executive functions: inhibition (self-control, selective attention), working memory, and cognitive flexibility; reviews development, measurement and training.
Stress, poor sleep, loneliness and lack of exercise impair EFs.
athar_applications: Cognitive flexibility in ATHAR = switching hypotheses/perspectives when evidence changes; operationalize as time-to-revise after a disconfirming clue.
Avoid overloading working memory: provide an evidence board so reasoning, not memory, is tested.
limitations: EF training transfer is contested (cf. ATH-SRC-0533); review not a meta-analysis.

title: Counterfactual Thought
title_ar: التفكير المضاد للواقع
key_findings: Review: people spontaneously imagine 'if only' and 'what if' alternatives; counterfactuals explain the past, prepare for the future, implicate causal relations, and shape intentions, emotions (regret, relief) and moral judgments such as blame.
The ability develops through childhood and supports reasoning about others' (false) beliefs; knowledge affects which counterfactuals seem plausible.
athar_applications: Counterfactual probe pattern: 'If the suspect had left at 9 instead of 10, which clue would be different?' tests causal model understanding.
limitations: Abstract read (2026-10-27 gap-fill); Annual Review lists volume 67 (2016), OpenAlex lists online 2015.

title: Causality in Thought
title_ar: السببية في التفكير
key_findings: Causal Bayesian networks are the best normative framework but incomplete as a description of human causal thinking.
Three hallmarks beyond probabilistic dependency: mechanism, narrative, and mental simulation; simulations of several actors combine into narratives.
athar_applications: Players naturally reason through stories and mechanisms: ATHAR should let them build a causal timeline/mechanism and then test it against evidence.
Correlation-vs-causation cases should ask for a mechanism, not just a statistic.
limitations: Narrative reasoning can also mislead (coherent but false stories); ATHAR should include coherent-but-wrong narratives.

title: Critical Thinking: A Statement of Expert Consensus for Purposes of Educational Assessment and Instruction. Research Findings and Recommendations (The Delphi Report)
title_ar: التفكير النقدي: بيان إجماع الخبراء لأغراض التقييم والتعليم (تقرير دلفي)
key_findings: Delphi process with 46 experts (about half philosophers, the rest from education, social and physical sciences) produced a consensus statement on critical thinking for assessment and instruction (112 pages).
Covers both a cognitive-skill dimension and a dispositional dimension, plus recommendations for instruction and assessment; the specific skill list was not extracted in this session.
athar_applications: Widely used consensus anchor for defining CT to schools and ministries; map ATHAR's taxonomy onto its skill and disposition dimensions in partner-facing documents.
Reported conceptual basis of the commercial CCTST/CCTDI (Insight Assessment) — not verified in this session.
limitations: Expert opinion (Delphi), not empirical validation; North American, philosophy-heavy panel.
Sub-skill list not verified in full text; do not quote specific sub-skills until checked.

title: Thinking and Deciding
title_ar: التفكير واتخاذ القرار
edition_version: 4th edition (Crossref metadata says 2006; abstract says first published 2007). A newer edition may exist; not verified.
key_findings: Standard academic textbook on the psychology of thinking and decision making (bibliographic record verified; content not re-read in this session).

Baron is associated with the construct of actively open-minded thinking (AOT), used as a disposition measure in Stanovich-Toplak research (see ATH-SRC-0515) — association from domain knowledge; check in full text.
athar_applications: Designer reference for normative vs descriptive vs prescriptive framing: debriefs should state which normative standard defines the 'right' answer.
AOT (searching for evidence against favored possibilities) as a target disposition.
limitations: Content claims rely on general knowledge of the book; edition currency not confirmed (check for a 5th edition).

title: The Rationality Quotient: Toward a Test of Rational Thinking
title_ar: معامل العقلانية: نحو اختبار للتفكير العقلاني
key_findings: Presents the Comprehensive Assessment of Rational Thinking (CART), a prototype test meant to parallel IQ tests but measure rationality (480 pp.).
CART targets probabilistic and scientific reasoning, avoidance of miserly information processing, and the knowledge structures (mindware) that support rational thought.
athar_applications: CART's architecture is the best available map of rational-thinking components distinct from intelligence; ATHAR's taxonomy cross-references it.
Items are copyrighted: conceptual reference only; ATHAR builds original items.
limitations: Long prototype test; mainly North American samples; third-party licensing of the full instrument not verified.
The rationality-vs-IQ distinction is debated (not reviewed here).

title: Watson-Glaser Critical Thinking Appraisal (official product page)
title_ar: اختبار واتسون-جليسر لتقييم التفكير النقدي
key_findings: 40 items, 30-40 minutes; five subtests (inference, recognising assumptions, deduction, interpretation, evaluation of arguments) reported as Recognize Assumptions, Evaluate Arguments, Draw Conclusions.
Used for recruitment and development; requires qualified users (BPS Level A training outside US/Canada).
Languages listed: English (UK/US), French, French Canadian, Dutch, Spanish, Latin American Spanish — Arabic not listed.
athar_applications: Not suitable as ATHAR's outcome measure (occupational, commercial, no Arabic); possible licensed external check in an 18+ pilot.
Informs micro-item formats only; items must never be copied or paraphrased.
limitations: Vendor page: no independent validity data shown; psychometrics must come from manuals or peer review (not verified here).

title: Halpern Critical Thinking Assessment (HCTA) — official test listing
title_ar: تقييم هالبرن للتفكير النقدي
key_findings: Five dimensions (verbal reasoning, argument analysis, thinking as hypothesis testing, likelihood and uncertainty, decision making and problem solving), each with five everyday scenarios.
Standard forms combine assessor-scored open responses (45-80 min); short forms are multiple choice (15-25 min); parallel forms; Rasch-conforming; norms 18+ from a convenience sample.
athar_applications: Closest commercial analogue to ATHAR's approach: everyday scenarios, open response then forced choice — inspires a two-step 'explain, then choose' item format.
Dimensions map onto ATHAR domains B, C, E; any validation use needs a license.
limitations: Licensing terms not on page; no Arabic version confirmed; adult norms only.

title: Halpern Critical Thinking Assessment Predicts Real-World Outcomes of Critical Thinking
key_findings: 133 US participants (community adults n=50, state-university n=48, community-college n=35) completed the HCTA and a behavioral inventory of negative life events.
Higher HCTA scores correlated with fewer reported negative life events (r = -.38).
athar_applications: Template for ATHAR's long-term criterion validation: relate reasoning scores to self-reported real-life decisions, cautiously.
limitations: Small, correlational, self-report outcomes; CT not separated from education, SES or intelligence; author is in Halpern's circle (check interests).

title: Real-World Correlates of Performance on Heuristics and Biases Tasks in a Community Sample
key_findings: Community adult sample; tasks: ratio bias, belief bias, syllogistic reasoning, cognitive reflection, probabilistic/statistical reasoning, temporal discounting; dispositions: actively open-minded thinking, future orientation, superstitious thinking.
Measures were modestly associated with fewer negative real-world outcomes (substance use, driving, finances, gambling, media use, computer security) and predicted outcomes beyond education and sex.
athar_applications: Bias-task performance and dispositions carry a modest real-world signal: worth tracking, not over-claiming.
limitations: Correlational; self-reported outcomes; modest associations; print year should be confirmed (Crossref volume 30).

title: The Cognitive Reflection Test as a predictor of performance on heuristics-and-biases tasks
key_findings: The CRT predicted performance on a wide set of heuristics-and-biases tasks better than measures of cognitive ability, thinking dispositions and executive functioning.

Despite a substantial correlation with cognitive ability, the CRT remained a unique predictor after controlling for the other measures; authors attribute this to its capturing a tendency toward miserly processing.
athar_applications: Supports treating reflective-override items as one component of an ATHAR composite, not the whole measure.
limitations: Abstract read via PubMed (2026-10-27 gap-fill); adult (university) samples; CRT items are widely known, so familiarity can inflate scores.

title: The cognitive reflection test is robust to multiple exposures
key_findings: Six studies (~2,500 participants, 17 variables): prior CRT exposure raised scores but did not significantly reduce the CRT's predictive power (abstract via the PsyArXiv preprint record).
athar_applications: Familiarity inflates raw scores even if predictive validity survives: ATHAR must use original, unexposed items to measure learning gains.
limitations: Adult online samples; predictive validity is not the same as validity for measuring change.

title: Assessing Critical Thinking in Higher Education: Current State and Directions for Next-Generation Assessment
key_findings: Reviews CT definitions across higher-education and workforce frameworks, existing assessments and their psychometric qualities, and design/implementation challenges.
Proposes an operational CT definition and key considerations for next-generation CT assessment.
athar_applications: Cite when explaining to partners why ATHAR builds its own scenario-based assessment instead of adopting a single commercial test.
limitations: US higher-education focus; instrument-level conclusions not extracted in this session.

title: Critical thinking Assessment Test (CAT) — Tennessee Tech Center for Assessment & Improvement of Learning
authors: Tennessee Tech University, Center for Assessment & Improvement of Learning
key_findings: Mostly short-answer test emulating real-world problems; developed with faculty input; NSF-funded (grants 0404911, 0717654, 1022789).
Used by 350+ institutions; faculty engage with real student responses; training and statistical support provided.
athar_applications: Model for rubric-scored constructed responses and for training human/AI scorers of ATHAR's open 'case report'.
limitations: Official page gives no psychometric data or license terms; validity evidence must be sought in technical reports (not verified).

title: The Elements of Reasoning and the Intellectual Standards
title_ar: عناصر الاستدلال والمعايير الفكرية
key_findings: Eight elements of reasoning: purpose, question, assumptions, point of view, information/evidence, concepts, inferences/conclusions, implications/consequences.
Seven intellectual standards applied to each element: clarity, precision, accuracy, relevance, depth, breadth, logic.
FCT requires written permission (with exact proposed changes) for use; prefers its theory not be reworded; research approval conditional on sharing findings.
athar_applications: Checklist inspiration for debrief prompts ('what assumption did you make?') in ATHAR's own wording; no reproduction of FCT text or diagrams without permission.
Restrictive terms make it unsuitable as ATHAR's named framework in a commercial product.
limitations: Practitioner framework; independent empirical validation not found in this session.

title: Critical Thinking and Subject Specificity: Clarification and Needed Research
key_findings: Distinguishes three versions of subject specificity (domain, epistemological, conceptual), finds the first two useful, argues key terms are too vague, and sets a research agenda.
Widely cited as the source of the general / infusion / immersion / mixed typology of CT instruction used by Abrami et al. (typology from secondary use; verify in full text).
athar_applications: Frames ATHAR's 'mixed' approach: explicit general principles plus immersion in case content.
limitations: Conceptual paper; typology details need full-text confirmation.

title: The Skills of Argument
title_ar: مهارات الحجة
key_findings: Classic interview study of everyday argument skills (bibliographic record verified; content not re-read in this session).
Commonly cited for showing that many people struggle to give genuine evidence, alternative theories, counterarguments and rebuttals for their own causal theories (domain knowledge; verify in text).
athar_applications: Kuhn's argument components (genuine evidence vs pseudo-evidence, alternative theories, counterargument, rebuttal) are a ready rubric for ATHAR's final case report.
limitations: Content claims flagged for full-text check; 1991 US samples.

title: Dialogic Argumentation as a Vehicle for Developing Young Adolescents' Thinking
title_ar: الحِجاج الحواري وسيلةً لتنمية تفكير المراهقين الصغار
key_findings: Multiyear study with two cohorts of young adolescents using electronic peer dialogues on social issues.

Dialogue groups transferred the skill to individual essays on new topics, outperforming comparison groups that did extensive essay writing and whole-class discussion, and better recognized how evidence relates to argument.
athar_applications: Strongest teen-specific evidence in this library: sustained structured dialogue (not essay drills) builds argument skill that transfers to new topics.
Classroom/multiplayer mode: paired opposing-side text dialogues about case conclusions.
limitations: One program and setting; quasi-experimental cohorts; multi-year dosage far above casual app use.

title: Improving analytical reasoning and argument understanding: a quasi-experimental field study of argument visualization
title_ar: تحسين الاستدلال التحليلي وفهم الحجج: دراسة ميدانية لتصوير الحجج
key_findings: 12-week undergraduate seminar practicing software-based argument visualization.
Seminar students improved more on LSAT Logical Reasoning forms than controls (d = 0.71, 95% CI 0.37-1.04) and wrote better blind-scored essays in a parallel course (d = 0.87, 95% CI 0.26-1.48).
athar_applications: Supports an argument-map mechanic for the final accusation and for dissecting NPC arguments.
Gains came from sustained intensive practice with feedback; a few in-game maps will not reproduce them.
limitations: Quasi-experimental, self-selected seminar at a highly selective university; small sample; intensive instructor feedback confounded with mapping.

title: Feedback exercises boost discernment of misinformation for gamified inoculation interventions
title_ar: تمارين التغذية الراجعة تعزز التمييز في تدخلات التحصين المُلعَّبة
key_findings: Addresses concerns that inoculation games lower trust in real news and decay: two preregistered lab experiments (N=191, N=321) plus four in-game quasi-experiments (hundreds to ~2,558 players each).

Feedback exercises after Bad News / Harmony Square improved discernment of both misinformation and real news (one week later in the lab), mainly via better accuracy on real news; confirmed with signal detection analysis.
athar_applications: Gameplay alone can teach blanket distrust; feedback exercises on true AND false items restore discernment.
Every ATHAR credibility module ends with a short scored feedback exercise that includes trustworthy items.
limitations: Authored by the inoculation group (interest in outcome); quasi-experimental in-game samples; exact N per study 3-6 to be checked in full text.

title: Many Labs 2: Investigating Variation in Replicability Across Samples and Settings
publisher: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 1(4), 443-490
key_findings: 28 findings, ~125 samples, 15,305 participants, 36 countries/territories: 15 (54%) replicated at p<.05.
Median d fell from 0.60 (originals) to 0.15 (replications); 75% of replication effects were smaller than the originals.
Little heterogeneity by lab vs online or WEIRD vs less-WEIRD samples; variation depended mainly on the effect itself.
athar_applications: Default skepticism rule: expect published effects to shrink; never present a single-study effect as fact in teaching content.
When effects are real they tended to hold across cultures — mildly encouraging for Arab-region use.
limitations: Which judgment/decision effects were included not extracted here; check before citing per-bias results.

title: Psychological Strategies for Winning a Geopolitical Forecasting Tournament
title_ar: استراتيجيات نفسية للفوز في بطولة تنبؤ جيوسياسي
key_findings: Two-year geopolitical forecasting tournament: training in probabilistic reasoning (reference classes, debiasing, averaging estimates), teaming, and tracking top performers each improved calibration and resolution.
The group produced the best forecasts in both years.
athar_applications: Real-world evidence that short probabilistic-reasoning training improves calibrated judgment on novel, genuinely uncertain questions.
Supports confidence scoring with proper scoring rules (Brier), reference-class prompts and team deliberation in ATHAR.
limitations: Adult volunteers; training was one part of a multi-component system; effect sizes not extracted in this session.

title: Learning and transfer: A general role for analogical encoding
title_ar: التعلم والنقل: دور عام للترميز القياسي
key_findings: Three studies with novices learning negotiation strategies: analogical learning beat no case study; comparing two cases side by side gave a marked advantage over studying them separately; more support increased transfer to a live negotiation.
athar_applications: After two cases sharing a reasoning structure, ATHAR asks players to compare them explicitly ('what is the same?').
Canonical owner probably Learning Science (07); cataloged here because it underpins transfer design rules.
limitations: Negotiation domain, adult learners; evidence-reasoning domain untested.

title: The effects of statistical training on thinking about everyday problems
title_ar: أثر التدريب الإحصائي على التفكير في المشكلات اليومية
key_findings: Four experiments supporting the view that rules for the law of large numbers are not tied to one content domain and can be improved by formal teaching; statistical training improved everyday reasoning (ERIC abstract).
athar_applications: If confirmed, a counterweight to pessimistic far-transfer claims for statistical principles; supports rule + varied-examples design for RS-12.
limitations: Short ERIC abstract only; effect sizes and which training formats worked best not extracted; 1986 US samples.

title: Giving Debiasing Away: Can Psychological Research on Correcting Cognitive Errors Promote Human Welfare?
key_findings: Argues confirmation bias contributes to ideological extremism and asks whether public debiasing could help.
Reviews known and unknown debiasing techniques and the barriers to real-world use; calls combating extreme confirmation bias a priority for psychology.
athar_applications: Frames ATHAR's social mission credibly while acknowledging that real-world debiasing evidence was thin before 2015.
limitations: Position paper; predates the stronger game-based evidence (ATH-SRC-0517/0518).

title: Civic Online Reasoning curriculum (Digital Inquiry Group)
title_ar: منهج التفكير المدني الرقمي
license: Mixed per item: CC BY 4.0 (e.g., Lateral Reading, Evaluating Data, Sponsored Content lessons) and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (e.g., social media assessments, several history lessons, professional learning)
key_findings: Free lessons and assessments built on three questions: who is behind the information, what is the evidence, what do other sources say.
Licensing is item-specific: some lessons CC BY 4.0 (commercial adaptation with attribution), many assessments CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (no commercial use, no derivatives).
athar_applications: CC BY 4.0 items (e.g., Lateral Reading lesson) may be adapted into Arabic for ATHAR with attribution — verify each item's license first.
BY-NC-ND assessments cannot be translated/adapted for the commercial product; design inspiration only.
limitations: Site does not itself state the Stanford connection; per-item license must be checked; US-centric examples.

title: California Critical Thinking Skills Test (CCTST) - product page
key_findings: Vendor describes the CCTST as calibrated for undergraduate and graduate students; 40 scenario-based items in 55 minutes, administered online.
Reports 8 skill scores (analysis, interpretation, inference, evaluation, explanation, induction, deduction, numeracy) plus an OVERALL score on 100-point scales with qualitative bands.
Vendor lists an Arabic-language version among 18 languages; price by quote.
Vendor classes CCTST and CCTDI as 'legacy' tools on its products page.
athar_applications: Candidate licensed external criterion for an adult or late-teen validation sample, since an Arabic version exists; not suitable for 13-15 (college calibration).
limitations: Vendor claims of validity and reliability are not independently verified here.
An independent content critique judged 9 of 34 items in the 1990 form defective (ATH-SRC-0571); later forms not examined.

title: How can critical thinking be assessed? (annotated list of critical thinking tests, incl. Cornell Critical Thinking Tests Levels X and Z and the Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test)
key_findings: Cornell Critical Thinking Test Level X (Ennis & Millman, 2005; The Critical Thinking Company): grades 4-14, multiple choice; induction, credibility, observation, deduction, assumption identification; 5th-edition manual (2005).
Cornell Level Z: college and adults, usable with advanced high-school students; adds prediction and experimental planning, fallacies (equivocation), definition.

Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test (1985): grades 7 through college; open-ended argument appraisal; discontinued by the original publisher but downloadable at no cost with a 2005 supplement of norms and reliability data.
The same page lists the CCTST (college level) and CCTDI.
athar_applications: Cornell Level X is the only verified multiple-choice CT instrument here whose stated range covers ATHAR's 13-15 band; Ennis-Weir offers a free open-response criterion for argument appraisal (ages 13+).
limitations: Author's own descriptive listing (potential interest); Cornell tests are commercial and the publisher page could not be loaded (JavaScript gate). No Arabic versions confirmed.

title: Supplement to the Test/Manual entitled The Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test
publisher: Illinois Critical Thinking Project, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (hosted on CriticalThinking.NET)
key_findings: Compiles user norms and 'reliability' indices: inter-rater values mostly about .72 to .99 for high-school and college groups; lower (.58-.61) for non-gifted 5th-6th graders, whom the author judged too young for the test.
Cronbach's alpha (.59 college, .72 high school) is reported but the author argues alpha is ill-suited to a multidimensional essay test.
Author warns that high reliability says nothing about validity, and supports validity with content arguments and experimental gains after explicit CT instruction.
athar_applications: An open-response rubric-scored criterion with documented human inter-rater agreement: a benchmark for what agreement ATHAR's human or LLM scorers should reach on Arabic justifications (after translation and adaptation, subject to permission).
limitations: Developer-compiled, mostly small US samples; no Arabic adaptation; permission for translation not established.

title: Jordanian TEFL Graduate Students' Use of Critical Thinking Skills (as Measured by the Cornell Critical Thinking Test, Level Z)
publisher: International Journal of Bilingual Education and Bilingualism 9(1), 33-50
key_findings: 50 MA TEFL students at Yarmouk University (Jordan) took the Cornell Level Z; they performed quite poorly overall.
Gender, age and GPA were associated with scores (per ERIC abstract).
athar_applications: Rare Arab-sample use of a standard CT test; shows that Arab adult samples can score low on an English-language CT test, so language and test format must be separated from the construct in ATHAR's validation.
limitations: Small adult sample; test administered in English to EFL students, confounding language proficiency with critical thinking; abstract-level reading only.

title: Examining the Exam: A Critical Look at the California Critical Thinking Skills Test
key_findings: Content (not statistical) review of the 1990 CCTST: judged 9 of its 34 questions defective because they themselves contain reasoning errors.
Concludes scores can indicate at most minimal competency on the skills tested, not an adequate measure of critical thinking.
athar_applications: Item-level logic review by philosophers/logicians should be a gate for ATHAR's own items, independent of psychometric statistics.
limitations: Concerns the 1990 form; later revisions not assessed; abstract-level reading only.

title: Meta-Analysis of Argument Visualization Tools in Higher Education: Examining Effects on Student Achievement and Moderating Factors
key_findings: PRISMA meta-analysis: 14 studies, 20 effect sizes, N = 1,455 higher-education students.
Unadjusted pooled effect was large (g about 1.59) but publication-bias analyses indicated inflation; bias-adjusted estimate about g = 0.87.

Gains were larger for argumentative essay quality than for standardized critical-thinking measures; larger for EFL/non-English cohorts; specialised mapping platforms and scaffolded, focused familiarisation beat minimal LMS-embedded use; no difference by design type.
athar_applications: Supports a light, scaffolded argument-map/claim template, introduced in short focused sessions.
Expect smaller effects on general CT tests than on task-specific argument quality: measure both, and do not market CT gains from map practice alone.
limitations: Higher-education samples only; small number of studies; journal DOI not confirmed (a preprint DOI 10.2139/ssrn.5643672 exists); read at abstract level via ERIC.

title: Argument Mapping in Higher Education: A Systematic Review
key_findings: Coded 124 studies (102 empirical) on postsecondary argument mapping: 44% assessed attitudes, 40% collaborative mapping, 51% quality/structure of student maps.
The most frequently studied causal question was the effect of mapping on critical-thinking skills; the review assesses prospects for meta-analysis rather than pooling effects.
athar_applications: Evidence base is mostly attitudes and map quality, not transfer; ATHAR should treat map-based CT gains as a hypothesis to test.
limitations: Postsecondary only; descriptive review without pooled estimate; abstract-level reading.

title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of educational approaches to reduce cognitive biases among students
key_findings: 54 RCTs (383 effect sizes, 10,941 participants): educational debiasing produced a small significant reduction in committing biases vs control (g = 0.26, 95% CI 0.14-0.39; 160 effects from 41 studies).
Most interventions targeted biases such as confirmation bias with cognitive strategies; some biases (e.g., representativeness) seemed hard to overcome.
All studies had unclear or high risk of bias, with some publication-bias risk; depth and transfer beyond class tasks remain open questions.
athar_applications: Calibrates expectations: plan for small average effects (g about 0.2-0.3) on targeted tasks, not the 24-32% reductions of single strong studies (ATH-SRC-0517).
Representativeness cases need extra scaffolding and should not be used as headline proof of effect.
limitations: Abstract-level reading; students of mixed ages, mostly not Arab samples; transfer to real decisions untested.

title: A signal detection theory meta-analysis of psychological inoculation against misinformation
key_findings: Re-analysed 33 inoculation experiments (combined N about 37,025) with signal detection theory in a hierarchical Bayesian model.
Reports that gamified and video interventions improved discrimination between reliable and unreliable news without shifting response bias (no general increase in scepticism).
Authors disclose that one co-author co-created some of the gamified interventions analysed.
athar_applications: Qualifies, but does not overturn, the discernment-first rule: inoculation can improve discrimination; ATHAR should still score discernment and bias separately and report both.
limitations: Authored partly by intervention developers (declared); conflicts with the earlier reanalysis ATH-SRC-0523, and a methods critique was published of a separate JMIR inoculation meta-analysis (Lu et al. 2023; DOI 10.2196/64430). Abstract-level reading.
